claims: Dynamic warm-up literature concerns a category of activity rather than an exact knee-hug movement.

Vortex defines this candidate by its observable alternating walk, single-leg stance, controlled ipsilateral knee-to-chest hand hold, release, and step-through; it does not include a calf raise, hop, run, or balance assessment.
Warm-up effects depend on the activity sequence and subsequent task.
This is a sagittal-plane, alternating locomotor mobility task with an upper-body-assisted hip-flexion hold; adding plantarflexion, a pause test, or another gait pattern changes the contract.
Acute stretching evidence addresses range-of-motion responses rather than isolated-muscle activation claims.
The card records hip flexors, gluteal and hamstring tissues, quadriceps, calf, foot, trunk, and shoulder/elbow roles as task anatomy without diagnosis or guaranteed tissue change.
Dynamic stretching is performed through movement rather than a sustained passive position.
A valid cycle requires stance organization, an ipsilateral knee-hug hold within comfortable range, release, and a controlled step-through before the other side.
General and activity-specific warm-up conditions should not be treated as identical exposures.
Candidate scores assess only the exercise's coordination and physical demand; they do not classify an athlete by skill, age, experience, or eligibility.
Acute stretching effects and outcomes depend on type, dose, timing, and surrounding activity.
Track steps, sides, holds, range, support use, symptoms, and downstream balance or locomotor work instead of asserting a universal recovery interval or outcome.
Instruction, supervision, environment, and progressive exposure are relevant safeguards in supervised exercise.
Use a clear level lane, controlled pace, available support, communication, and an exit path; no demographic or proficiency classification is encoded on this exercise card.
Dynamic-stretching dose and performance evidence varies across protocols.
Candidate sets, steps, and hold durations are planning proposals only; stop before range is forced, posture degrades, or the drill becomes conditioning.
Activity-specific warm-up implementation matters to the task that follows.
Cue a controlled alternating walk, tall stance, comfortable knee-to-chest hold, release, and step-through without promising flexibility, injury prevention, or performance transfer.
Safe training requires appropriate instruction, supervision, and environment.
Stop for pain, new neurologic/circulatory symptoms, dizziness, unsafe balance or lane conditions, inability to communicate, or a participant stop request.
Stretching effects should be interpreted with dose and subsequent dynamic activity in view.
Use this only as a candidate preparation movement after the selected session inputs, logistics, duration, fatigue, substitutions, and downstream demands are validated.
Dynamic movement can be coached without framing a single drill as a guaranteed performance intervention.
Athlete support uses a simple range, balance, breathing, and stop-signal check; a support option or different reviewed task is acceptable when quality is not available.
Warm-up components should be considered in context rather than as universal prescriptions.
Coaches observe the side sequence, stance control, pelvic/trunk compensation, hand pressure, range, support use, pace, symptoms, and first loss of quality without diagnosing restriction.
Instruction and safe environments are core implementation safeguards.
Captions, transcript, still sequence, clear lane markers, support, verbal cueing, and a different reviewed movement remain candidate supports; media accessibility is not assumed.
Dynamic movement categories include differing tasks and do not establish equivalence between their mechanics.
The alternate review separates stance, hand assistance, locomotion, action order, added calf raise, external support, pause/testing intent, and range from the base walk-and-hug contract.
Task-specific instruction and supervision remain relevant to safe implementation.
Three oEmbed-metadata candidates are retained as candidates only; playback, mechanics, captions, accessibility, quality, and exact-match approval require human review.

assessmentSummary.identity: One Walking Knee Hug cycle is a controlled forward step, an organized single-leg stance, an ipsilateral knee-to-chest hand-assisted hold within a comfortable range, release, and step-through to the other side. It is not a static standing stretch, knee-hug-to-calf-raise sequence, walking quad pull, high-knee march, lunge, hop, balance assessment, or running drill.
currentCardFindings: Source 50 describes only a generic walk-and-knee-pull sequence; it omits side and cycle boundaries, hold/release, range, support, lane, fatigue, substitutions, and current review status.

The established identity boundary correctly keeps Walking Knee Hug separate from Walking Knee Hug to Calf Raise because plantarflexion, balance exposure, action order, and repetition boundary are added.

Three legacy YouTube candidates returned oEmbed metadata on 2026-08-09. Exact mechanics, playback, captions, accessibility, instructional quality, current availability, and approval remain human-review work.

proposedLoadProfile.recovery: candidate planning estimate only; recompute from actual steps, holds, pace, range, support, symptoms, and overlapping work

proposedDosage.prepare: 1-3 controlled passes or 4-10 cycles per side with range and pace held below compensation
proposedDosage.rest: walk-back or pause until balance, breathing, symptoms, and intended range are acceptable
proposedDosage.durationRule: include lane, cueing, support setup, side count, pauses, substitutions, cleaning, exit, and downstream session timing

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when a clear level lane or safe stationary alternative, comfortable range, controlled single-leg stance, communication, support if needed, session duration, fatigue, logistics, substitutions, and downstream demands fit. Recompute selection, dosage, fatigue, logistics, substitution, persistence, and coach/athlete rendering after any change.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Dynamic-stretching and warm-up reviews, source-card audit, and the recorded boundary against Walking Knee Hug to Calf Raise.
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: The evidence does not establish a universal hold duration, range, step count, recovery interval, readiness threshold, clinical eligibility, or Vortex score. Human review is required for every score, relationship, and video.
